opus-5.5.text:
I think it's not that I completely distrust it, but I've learned to be suspicious of it. When you just sit in your office and think really hard, the ideas that come out tend to be the ones that feel elegant in your head. They're clean, they make a nice story, and you can already imagine the paper. But very often they're disconnected from what's actually happening in the data or in the models. You end up solving a problem that you invented, rather than a problem that really exists.

For me, the best research ideas almost always come from getting your hands dirty. You run experiments, you look at the failure cases, you stare at the visualizations, and something surprises you. Something doesn't behave the way you expected. That moment of surprise is where the real idea is, because it means reality is telling you something your intuition didn't already know. If you only think, you can never be surprised by yourself.

There's also a deeper issue, which is that in deep learning especially, our intuitions are often wrong. Many things that "should" work don't, and many things that seem too simple or even stupid turn out to work extremely well. If you filter ideas purely through reasoning, you'll throw away exactly those simple things, because they don't sound clever enough. So I'd rather have a fast loop: a rough idea, try it, look carefully at what happens, and let the empirical signal shape where you go next.

And honestly, thinking is cheap in a way that can be a trap. It feels productive. You can spend weeks refining a beautiful framework without ever testing whether the core assumption holds. I tell my students: don't fall in love with the idea before you've seen the first plot. The thinking should come after you have something real to think about.

r001.rationale: The response warns that solitary thinking can produce elegant but ungrounded ideas; it does not say that a brilliant, unprecedented idea from solitary reflection is extremely unlikely.

r002.rationale: It does not state that many people are likely to conceive the same idea independently at the same time.

r003.rationale: It does not identify rediscovering an idea that others have repeatedly tried as a risk.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I've been burned by it enough times. Early on, I'd sit at my desk, think very hard, and come up with what felt like a beautiful idea. Elegant, principled, the kind of thing you want to put on a slide. And then you actually run it, and the data just doesn't care. The model doesn't care about how elegant your intuition was.

So over time I've come to believe that the ideas that actually survive almost never arrive fully formed in your head. They come from being in the loop with the system. You train something, you look at what it's doing, something looks weird, you poke at it, and that weirdness becomes the research question. Most of the work I'm proud of started that way, not from a whiteboard.

Part of it is also humility about our intuitions. These models operate at a scale where human intuition is a pretty unreliable guide. We have strong priors from decades of computer vision, and a lot of those priors turned out to be wrong, or at least unnecessary, once you had enough data and compute. If you only reason from your priors, you tend to rediscover your own biases.

That doesn't mean thinking is useless. You need taste to know which weird thing is worth chasing. But I tell my students: don't trust an idea until you've touched the data. Build the smallest version, see what breaks, and let the experiment argue back. The best research is a conversation with the system, not a monologue in your head.

r001.rationale: The response says solitary ideas may fail when tested, but does not say that a brilliant idea no one else has conceived is extremely unlikely.

r002.rationale: It does not state that many people are likely to independently think of the same idea at the same time.

r003.rationale: It mentions rediscovering one’s own biases, but not the risk of repeating an idea others have already tried repeatedly.

astra-6.text:
I’m skeptical of ideas that sound convincing before you’ve actually tried anything. When you’re just sitting and thinking, it’s easy to build a story around assumptions you haven’t tested. The story can be very elegant, but that doesn’t mean the assumptions are right.

For me, the useful thinking happens in a loop with experiments. You implement something, look at the results, and discover that the model behaves differently from what you expected. Then you have a concrete question: why did that happen? That question can lead somewhere you wouldn’t have reached by thinking alone.

So it’s not that thinking isn’t important. It’s that I don’t trust the elegance of an idea as evidence that it’s good. I want to see what happens when it meets an actual problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m skeptical because it’s very easy to convince yourself that an idea is good when it only exists in your head. You make assumptions, build a coherent story around them, and then mistake that coherence for evidence.

For me, the useful thinking happens in a loop with experiments. You try something, look at what actually happens, and discover that one of your assumptions was wrong. That surprise can lead to a much better question than the one you started with.

So I wouldn’t say thinking is unimportant. You need intuition to decide what to try. But I don’t trust the intuition until it has had some contact with reality. An elegant explanation is a starting point; it isn’t a result.
